notes.text: And Moses went up — When he knew the place of his death he cheerfully mounted a steep hill to come to it. Those who are well acquainted with another world, are not afraid to leave this. When God's servants are sent for out of the world, the summons runs go up and die! Unto Daniel - To that city which after Moses's death was called so.

All Naphtali — The land of Naphtali, which together with Daniel, was in the north of Canaan, as Ephraim and Manasseh were in the midland parts, and Judah on the south, and the sea, on the west. So these parts lying in the several quarters are put for all the rest. He stood in the east and saw also Gilead, which was in the eastern part of the land, and thence he saw the north and south and west. The utmost sea - The midland sea, which was the utmost bound of the land of promise on the west.

The south — The south quarter of the land of Judah, which is towards the salt sea, the city of palm-trees - Jericho, so called from the multitude of palm-trees, which were in those parts, as Josephus and Strabo write. From whence and the balm there growing it was called Jericho, which signifies, odouriferous or sweet smelling.

I have caused thee to see it — For tho' his sight was good, yet he could not have seen all Canaan, an hundred and sixty miles in length, and fifty or sixty in breadth, if his sight had not been miraculously assisted and enlarged. He saw it at a distance. Such a sight the Old Testament believers had of the kingdom of the Messiah. And such a sight believers have now of the glory that shall he revealed. Such a sight have we now, of the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, which shall cover the earth. Those that come after us shall undoubtedly enter into that promised land: which is a comfort to us, when we find our own carcases falling in this wilderness.

So Moses the servant of the Lord died — He is called the servant of the Lord, not only as a good man, (all such are his servants) but as a man eminently useful, who had served God's counsels in bringing Israel out of Egypt, and leading them thro' the wilderness. And it was more his honour, to be the servant of the Lord, than to be king in Jeshurun. Yet he dies. Neither his piety nor his usefulness would exempt him from the stroke of death. God's servants must die, that they may rest from their labours, receive their recompense, and make room for others. But when they go hence, they go to serve him better, to serve him day and night in his temple. The Jews say, God sucked his soul out of his body with a kiss. No doubt he died in the embraces of his love.

He — The Lord, buried him either immediately, or by the ministry of angels, whereof Michael was the chief or prince. Of his sepulchre - Of the particular place where he was buried: which God hid from the Israelites, to prevent their superstition and idolatry, to which he knew their great proneness. And for this very reason the devil endeavoured to have it known and contended with Michael about it, Jude i, 9. God takes care even of the dead bodies of his servants. As their death is precious, so is their dust. Not one grain of it shall be lost, but the covenant with it shall be remembered.
His eye was not dim — By a miraculous work of God in mercy to his church and people.

Thirty day's — Which was the usual time of mourning for persons of high place and eminency. 'Tis a debt owing to the surviving honour of deceased worthies, to follow them with our tears, as those who loved and valued them, are sensible of the loss, and humbled for the sins which have provoked God to deprive us of them.

Wisdom — And other gifts and graces too, but wisdom is mentioned as being most necessary for the government to which he was now called. Upon him - And this was the thing which Moses at that time asked of God for him.
Whom the Lord — Whom God did so freely and familiarly converse with.

Moses was greater than any other of the prophets of the Old Testament. By Moses God gave the law, and molded and formed the Jewish church. By the other prophets he only sent particular reproofs, directions and predictions. But as far as the other prophets came short of him, our Lord Jesus went beyond him. Moses was faithful as a servant, but Christ as a son: his miracles more illustrious, his communion with the father more intimate: for he is in his bosom from eternity. Moses lies buried: but Christ is sitting at the right-hand of God, and of the increase of his government there shall be no end.

glossa.text:
*He went up therefore.* Moses as well as the other fathers of the Old Testament, lifted up in spirit to the height of contemplation, were able to foresee the grace of the New Testament, which is given in Christ, both by the conferring of the virtues and by the receiving of the heavenly kingdom: but they could not await it in the flesh, and died in faith and hope, and were led down to the lower regions, where they awaited the coming of the Redeemer, who by the blood of his redemption should free them from thence.

*And he showed him.* Moses saw the land of promise, and did not enter it, because the law foreshadowed in words and figures the coming of Christ and the doctrine of the Gospel, but led no man to perfection.
*All the land.* A part of all the land, so much as he could see from the highest mountain. Or he showed him all the land in spirit.

*And he died there,* etc. God spares none of the elect, and avenges even the least sins, even in his friends; whence: *Moses and Aaron his priests,* and he added: *Thou wast propitious to them, and taking vengeance on all their inventions.* The law, namely, being ended, which served the Lord in its own time, the city was destroyed and the altar, nowhere sacrifices, nowhere libations, nowhere priest or pontiff.

*In a valley.* On the mountain he died, in a valley he was buried, because the law was glorious in its own time: but compared with the Gospel it seems hidden and lowly; whence: *I gave them precepts that were not good.*

*And no man hath known.* The Jews assert that this was done lest the Jews, ever prone to idolatry, should worship a dead man as God; but according to allegory it signifies that the time and manner of the ending of the law are hidden in the foreknowledge of God alone, and that neither the depth of the wisdom of God, nor the secret of his counsel, lies open to anyone, because his judgments are incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable.

*Moses was a hundred and twenty years old.* If from one, in the natural order, as far as fifteen, thou shalt join together the sums of the single numbers — one, that is, and two and three, and so onward — they make a hundred and twenty. And fifteen is made up of seven and eight: seven is referred to the sabbath, eight to circumcision, because on the eighth day the boy was circumcised. But if thou look to the New Testament, thou hast the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and in the eighth the resurrection of Christ; the hundred and twenty therefore signify those who even in the Old Testament strive to fulfil the precepts of the Law and of the Gospel.

*Moses was a hundred and twenty years old.* This signifies that he, as well as the other fathers of the Old Testament, after the perfection of the commandments of God, which is in the two precepts of charity, are through the grace of Christ and the redemption of his blood made fit for eternal rest and for the life to come; whose *eye was not dimmed,* the gaze, namely, of holy intention was not darkened with any cloud, nor were the *teeth* of malice *moved,* because their order of discretion was not disturbed by the tempest of the vices, a hundred and twenty are the years of the lawgiver, by which number the height of Solomon's temple was confirmed. The primitive Church also, after the passion and the resurrection and the Lord's ascension, received the grace of the Holy Spirit in this number of men. For fifteen, which is made up of seven and eight, signifies the life to come, which is now carried on in the sabbath of souls and shall be perfected in the resurrection of bodies. Fifteen also, brought into a triangle, that is, reckoned together with its own parts, makes a hundred and twenty. Fittingly therefore is the beatitude of the elect in the life to come signified by the hundred and the twenty, and the third upper room of the house of God is completed, because after the labours of the faithful, after the rest of souls, the full felicity of the Church shall be fulfilled in the glory of the resurrection.

*And they wept.* Because death reigned even in those who had not sinned, from Adam unto Moses: therefore tears follow him as he goes down to the lower regions.

((HIERON., epist. ad Paulam.)) It is no wonder if to Moses and Aaron, etc., *as far as* but to be within, that is, to minister to the will of the Lord.

*And they were completed.* From this the custom seems to have arisen, that for the faithful departed the offices of piety are discharged for thirty days.

*He laid upon him.* In his Scriptures he bore witness to him, saying: *God shall raise up a prophet,* etc. ((Deut. XVIII)), whence: *If you did believe Moses, you would perhaps believe me also ((Joan. V))*.

*And there arose not,* etc. This (as is reported) Esdras added of his own, who by a divine understanding restored the library burnt by the Chaldeans, and found the letters which the Jews now use, whence he was also called *a swift scribe* .

*And there arose not a prophet.* Because Moses was more excellent than all the prophets of the Old Testament: whence the Jews arrogantly say: *We are the disciples of Moses ((Joan. IX))*. But after the Lord of the prophets came incarnate into the world, all that former dignity and shadow of things to come ceased: because *the law and the figure was given by Moses: grace and truth by Jesus Christ, who is the end of the law unto justice to everyone that believeth ((Hebr. X; Joan. I; Rom. X))*.

*And he buried him in the valley.* The Lord, namely. And by this it is signified that, the hindrance of nature having been removed through Christ, the clean soul, once separated, ascends to God: and the body which is buried remains in the earth until the judgment. Ecclesiastes XII: Until the dust return into the dust whence it was, and the spirit return to God who gave it. Which return may he grant to be prosperous for us, who liveth and reigneth for ever and ever. *Amen.*

notes.text: Dwelling place — Although we and our fathers, for some generations, have had no fixed habitation, yet thou hast been instead of a dwelling-place to us, by thy watchful and gracious providence. And this intimates that all the following miseries were not to be imputed to God but themselves.
Thou — Thou hadst thy power, and all thy perfections, from all eternity.

Turnedst — But as for man, his case is far otherwise, though he was made by thee happy. and immortal, yet for his sin thou didst make him mortal and miserable. Saidst - Didst pronounce that sad sentence, return, O men, to the dust out of which ye were taken, Gen. iii, 19.
Past — Indeed time seems long when it is to come, but when it is past, very short and contemptible. A watch - Which lasted but three or four hours.
Them — Mankind. Away - Universally, without exception or distinction. A sleep - Short and vain, as sleep is, and not minded 'till it be past.

glossa.text:
*A prayer of Moses.* ((AUG.)) When the old life and the new, etc., *as far as* and he sees wonders out of the law of God.

((CASS., REM.)) This psalm treats of the failing of the human race, which shall be taken away through Christ.

*O Lord, a refuge.* ((CASS.)) First, he sets forth an eternal refuge for man in time.

*Before the mountains.* But lest he should seem not to have been, before he was a refuge to us, he adds *before. The mountains, the earth.* ((AUG.)) Behold, every rational creature is distinguished *Elcce* by this difference, that by the name *of mountains* is meant the loftiness of the angels; and by the name *of the earth* the lowliness of men: and therefore not unfittingly did he so distinguish the words, that he should say that *the mountains,* that is, the angels, *were made,* and that *the earth,* that is, men, *was formed. They should be made, or it should be formed.* To be formed, or fashioned, is wont to be said of bodies: to be made, out of nothing. *From the world.* He would more fitly say, etc., *as far as* but here *the world* is put for the eternal. *From the world.* Behold what eternity is a refuge to us, etc., *as far as: Turn not away, for a thousand years. Thou art.* Excellently does he say it, because he is unchangeable. He does not say thou shalt be, or thou wast, since the unchangeable essence of God has not known the past, or the future; whence it is said: *I am who am.* And, *He who is hath sent me to you?* And: *But thou art the selfsame, and thy years shall not fail.* *aani*

*Turn not away.* ((CASS.)) Secondly, he sets out the infirmity of man, for which he asks that help be brought. *Unto lowliness.* That is, earthly concupiscence, etc., *as far as* who taught us to seek the things of heaven.
*Yesterday's day.* ((AUG.)) He does not say, at least as tomorrow's, etc., *as far as* in anxiety, and trembling, as nothing *qnasi*.

*In the morning as grass.* ((AUG., CASS.)) Let it be changed from the quality of the night.

*In the evening let it fall.* Cut down, or broken, at the last. ((CASS.)) *In the morning as grass.* I have said that the years are held, etc., *as far as* the youth which flowers and passes away.

 *In the evening.* Old age, when the vigour of a man grows cold. *Or, in the morning as grass.* A fitting comparison, as if to say, as grass is changed from the quality which it has in the night, to a worse one in the morning when the sun is risen: so is a man changed for the worse.

notes.text: What was proposed, chap. i, 5, 6, is now more largely treated of: concerning Paul and his fellowlabourers, ver. 1-12; concerning the Thessalonians, ver. 13-16.
We had suffered — In several places. We are bold - Notwithstanding. With much contention - Notwithstanding both inward and outward conflicts of all kinds.

For our exhortation — That is, our preaching. A part is put for the whole. Is not, at any time, of deceit - We preach not a lie, but the truth of God. Nor of uncleanness - With any unholy or selfish view. This expression is not always appropriated to lust, although it is sometimes emphatically applied thereto. Nor in guile - But with great plainness of speech.

Flattering words — This ye know. Nor a cloak of covetousness - Of this God is witness. He calls men to witness an open fact; God, the secret intentions of the heart. In a point of a mixed nature, ver. 10, he appeals both to God and man.
Nor from others — Who would have honoured us more, if we had been burdensome - That is, taken state upon ourselves.
But we were gentle — Mild, tender. In the midst of you - Like a hen surrounded with her young. Even as a nurse cherisheth her own children - The offspring of her own womb.
To impart our own souls — To lay down our lives for your sake.

glossa.text: *That it was not.* This you know concerning it, that it was not in worldly prosperity, which is vain, but in much solicitude on account of adversities: and therefore we had confidence not in ourselves, who are frail, but in the Lord.
*At Philippi.* The affliction which he here calls to mind he suffered because of the pythonic spirit which he had cast out of the girl.

*Our exhortation.* Here he seems to begin against the false apostles, calling to mind the truth of the Gospel, then his prudent conversation among us. *In guile.* Even truth is in guile when it is preached not for the love of truth and the profit of the hearers, but that glory or some other gain may be acquired.

*Not as pleasing men.* Unless he himself work this in us, we cannot avoid it. For what strength to hurt the love of human glory has, he perceives not, save he who has declared war upon it: because, if it is easy for anyone not to covet praise while it is denied, it is nevertheless difficult not to be delighted with it when it is offered.

*Neither.* In this he touches the false apostles, who wished themselves rather than the doctrine of God to be commended. But the Apostle, who sought glory not for the present, but in the future, made himself lowly, that the preaching of God might be exalted. *In an occasion.* I say not, in covetousness, but neither did I do or say anything in which there might be an occasion of covetousness. Thence it is. *God is witness,* who knows the heart: for this is not so evident to men.

*We might have been to you,* etc. So far does he weigh down the cause of the false apostles that he says he refuses it, though it was lawful for him to seek supports for the restraining of those who had neither the means nor the shame of demanding. But the debt of apostolic power he calls a *burden,* because of the false apostles, who, usurping it unduly, exacted it importunately of the common people. *Her own children.* A woman sometimes nurses others' children for hire, not out of love: but her own, out of affection.

notes.text: Mark xii, 28; Luke x, 25.
A scribe asking him a question, trying him — Not, as it seems, with any ill design: but barely to make a further trial of that wisdom, which he had shown in silencing the Sadducees.
Deut. vi, 5.
Lev. xix, 18.
Luke xx, 41.
How doth David then by the Spirit — By inspiration, call him Lord? If he be merely the son (or descendant) of David? If he be, as you suppose, a mere man, the son of a man?

The Lord said to my Lord — This his dominion, to which David himself was subject, shows both the heavenly majesty of the king, and the nature of his kingdom. Sit thou on my right hand - That is, remain in the highest authority and power. Psalm cx, 1.
Neither durst any question him any more — Not by way of ensnaring or tempting him.

glossa.text: *Silence.* Note that the poisons of envy can be overcome, but with difficulty are laid to rest. *They came together.* That by their multitude they might overcome him whom they could not by reason. In tempting him those come together who in doctrine are contrary to one another. They had already been refuted in the showing of the penny, they had already seen the Sadducees too struck dumb, but yet ill-will and spite nourish shamelessness.

*Tempting him.* Mark says that the Lord said to him, when he had answered wisely: *Thou art not far from the kingdom of God.* For it could come to pass that he who came tempting was converted by the Lord's answer. Or the temptation is not an evil one, as of a man wishing to deceive, but by reason of a man wishing to try out further what he does not know.

*Thou shalt love the Lord thy God.* With his first answer the Lord strikes the feigned conscience of the questioner. *Thy God is one. Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain. Observe the day of the sabbath.* These three belong to the love of God: That thou shouldst think upon his unity, his truth, his will. *With thy whole heart.* The integrity of faith is expressed. In the whole soul, perfect obedience is required. In the whole mind, perseverance is shown.
*Of Christ.* Whether he has come, or whether you believe he is to come, whom you assert to be mere man.
*He said.* To say that is to beget a Son equal to himself. *To my Lord.* Not according to that whereby he was born of him, but according to that whereby he always was of the Father.
*How.* These things are contradictory according to your understanding.
*And no man could,* etc. Note that the poisons of envy can be overcome, but with difficulty are laid to rest.

notes.text: Be ye holy — Separated from all the forementioned defilements, and entirely consecrated to God and obedient to all his laws. I am holy - Both in my essence, and in all my laws, which are holy and just and good.

glossa.text: *The Lord spoke . . . Be ye holy. ((ORIG., hom. 12 in Lev.))* What this name which is "holy" signifies, etc., *as far as* namely, that ye may have your manner of life in the world.

notes.text: Blessed — The Hebrew words are very emphatical: O the blessedness of that man! Counsel - That doth not lead his life according to their counsel, or manner of living. Standeth - Which notes a more settled abode in it. Way - In their manner of conversation. Seat - Which notes a constant and resolved perseverance in their wicked courses. Scornful - Of those who make a mock of sin, and scoff at goodness and goodmen. Divers observe a gradation in this verse; the following clause still exceeding the former, for standing is more than walking, and sitting more than standing; and sinners in scripture use, are worse than the ungodly, and the scornful are the worst of sinners.
Day and night — Not seldom and slightly, but diligently, and constantly.
Whither — His happiness is not short and transitory, but, like those trees which are continually green and flourishing.
Ungodly — Their condition is far different. Chaff - They are restless and unquiet: their seeming felicity, hath no firm foundation, but quickly vanishes and flees away as chaff before the wind.
Not stand — Not endure the trial. Judgment - In the great and general judgment of the world.

Knoweth — He approves, loves, and delights in them, and therefore will recompence them. Perish - All their designs and courses shall come to nothing, and they shall perish with them. There is nothing in this psalm which is not applicable to Christ, but some things which are not all applicable to David. Threatenings denounced against the adversaries of Christ's kingdom, ver. 1-6. Promises made to Christ, ver. 7-9. Counsel given to all, to submit to him, ver. 10-12.

glossa.text: « Blessed is the man who hath not gone away, etc. » ((AUG., Enarr. in Psal., tom. III.)) The order, Adam went away when he withdrew from God; he stood, when he was delighted with sin; he sat, when, confirmed in pride, he could not return, save as set free by this man, who had none of these things. Adam went away when he consented to the persuasion of the devil; he stood, while he ate the apple; he sat, while he excused himself: « The woman whom thou gavest me seduced me. » ((Gen. III)) . After the likeness of exiles, who, while they are on the road, are more easily called back, while they now stand, with more difficulty: at length with the greatest difficulty, when they have there been made masters and lords. ((REMI.)) There is sinning by thought, by act, and by words in teaching. ((CASS.)) The impious man is so against God, the sinner against himself, the pestilent man against his neighbour. « In the chair, giving an example of sinning. » ((CASS.)) The throne is of kings, the tribunal of judges, the chair properly of teachers. ((Ibid.)) It is as though he said: You who have fallen through the first Adam, be ye conformed to this second one: because the blessed man is the contrary of the first

« But in the law. » AUG. ((CASS.)) Here he is shown full of every good in himself. ((AUG.)) It is not perfect praise to flee the things to be blamed, unless the things to be praised follow. In the order in which they grew in the first man, they are taken away in the second.

« In the law. » ((Ibid.)) He who is in the law acts according to the law, he who is under the law is acted upon according to the law: the one is free, the other a slave. ((Ibid. AMBR.)) One thing is the law which is written for him that serves, another that which is beheld with the mind by him who has no need of letters. « The will. » ((CASS.)) That there be no weariness of labour, nor idleness, but he shall meditate always. The will of sense is under the law; of reason, in the law; of divinity, above the law.

« And he shall be. » ((Ibid.)) Here he is shown useful to us, giving the fruit of life, and leaves, and overshadowing us, « Blessed is the man. But in the law. And he shall be. » The full definition of the blessed man. All these things belong not to every blessed man, but to Christ alone. « As a tree. » ((Ibid.)) After the likeness of the tree of life which is in paradise, whereof obedient man was to have eaten. « A tree. » ((Ibid.)) In paradise there is the tree of life, a tree unto life, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. « Of waters. » ((AUG.)) The waters are the Holy Spirit, according to that word: « He that shall have believed in me, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water ((Joan. VII)), » and it is against the heats of the vices. ((CASS.)) Or, by water, the wisdom of God, by which the inner man is restored, as thirst by water. ((AUG.)) Or the mortal race, as Job: « Many waters, many peoples, » because they flow down into death, as waters into the sea. « He shall give. » ((Ibid.)) To give pertains to the rational sense and to the will of the one offering. « And the leaf. » ((Ibid.)) As the leaves cover the fruit, so the words of the Lord guard his promises. « And all things. » ((Ibid.)) Why go through them one by one.

« Not so the impious. » Here by the vengeance upon the wicked he terrifies the adverse, the dread of these makes what has gone before more welcome. « From the face of the earth. » ((AUG.)) Of eternal stability, because as this earth nourishes and holds up a man, so that other earth holds up the inner man.

« Therefore they shall not rise again. » Because the wind casteth them away, that is, therefore, because they have been given over to a reprobate sense: therefore they do not rise again in the first resurrection, that they may judge themselves in counsel, that they may set the wills of God before their own. Or in the council, that is, in the harmonious multitude of the just, the impious idolaters, or apostates. Sinners, false Christians: or else therefore they do not rise again in the time to come, that they may judge, or that, being judged, they may rest in the council, that is, in the college of the just. « In judgment, etc. » In the judgment there will be four orders: some shall judge and shall not be judged, as the most perfect; some shall neither judge nor be judged, as the damned unbelievers; some shall be judged and shall be saved, as the moderately good; some shall be judged and shall perish, as the evil faithful. « In the council. » ((AUG.)) In the eternal good, to follow which was counsel to the saints. « Or in the council, » in the judgment, that they may judge together with them; for there is judgment when different sins are punished with different penalties; and it is said from this by likeness. « They rise again. » What resurrections these are: of the soul, from sins in the present; of the body, from death in the time to come, whereby it shall be made impassible and immortal.
« For the Lord knoweth, etc., » That is, these do not rise again in the soul, because God does not approve their works, but those of the just only.

notes.text: What was proposed, chap. i, 5, 6, is now more largely treated of: concerning Paul and his fellowlabourers, ver. 1-12; concerning the Thessalonians, ver. 13-16.
We had suffered — In several places. We are bold - Notwithstanding. With much contention - Notwithstanding both inward and outward conflicts of all kinds.

For our exhortation — That is, our preaching. A part is put for the whole. Is not, at any time, of deceit - We preach not a lie, but the truth of God. Nor of uncleanness - With any unholy or selfish view. This expression is not always appropriated to lust, although it is sometimes emphatically applied thereto. Nor in guile - But with great plainness of speech.

Flattering words — This ye know. Nor a cloak of covetousness - Of this God is witness. He calls men to witness an open fact; God, the secret intentions of the heart. In a point of a mixed nature, ver. 10, he appeals both to God and man.
Nor from others — Who would have honoured us more, if we had been burdensome - That is, taken state upon ourselves.
But we were gentle — Mild, tender. In the midst of you - Like a hen surrounded with her young. Even as a nurse cherisheth her own children - The offspring of her own womb.
To impart our own souls — To lay down our lives for your sake.

glossa.text: *That it was not.* This you know concerning it, that it was not in worldly prosperity, which is vain, but in much solicitude on account of adversities: and therefore we had confidence not in ourselves, who are frail, but in the Lord.
*At Philippi.* The affliction which he here calls to mind he suffered because of the pythonic spirit which he had cast out of the girl.

*Our exhortation.* Here he seems to begin against the false apostles, calling to mind the truth of the Gospel, then his prudent conversation among us. *In guile.* Even truth is in guile when it is preached not for the love of truth and the profit of the hearers, but that glory or some other gain may be acquired.

*Not as pleasing men.* Unless he himself work this in us, we cannot avoid it. For what strength to hurt the love of human glory has, he perceives not, save he who has declared war upon it: because, if it is easy for anyone not to covet praise while it is denied, it is nevertheless difficult not to be delighted with it when it is offered.

*Neither.* In this he touches the false apostles, who wished themselves rather than the doctrine of God to be commended. But the Apostle, who sought glory not for the present, but in the future, made himself lowly, that the preaching of God might be exalted. *In an occasion.* I say not, in covetousness, but neither did I do or say anything in which there might be an occasion of covetousness. Thence it is. *God is witness,* who knows the heart: for this is not so evident to men.

*We might have been to you,* etc. So far does he weigh down the cause of the false apostles that he says he refuses it, though it was lawful for him to seek supports for the restraining of those who had neither the means nor the shame of demanding. But the debt of apostolic power he calls a *burden,* because of the false apostles, who, usurping it unduly, exacted it importunately of the common people. *Her own children.* A woman sometimes nurses others' children for hire, not out of love: but her own, out of affection.

notes.text: Mark xii, 28; Luke x, 25.
A scribe asking him a question, trying him — Not, as it seems, with any ill design: but barely to make a further trial of that wisdom, which he had shown in silencing the Sadducees.
Deut. vi, 5.
Lev. xix, 18.
Luke xx, 41.
How doth David then by the Spirit — By inspiration, call him Lord? If he be merely the son (or descendant) of David? If he be, as you suppose, a mere man, the son of a man?

The Lord said to my Lord — This his dominion, to which David himself was subject, shows both the heavenly majesty of the king, and the nature of his kingdom. Sit thou on my right hand - That is, remain in the highest authority and power. Psalm cx, 1.
Neither durst any question him any more — Not by way of ensnaring or tempting him.

glossa.text: *Silence.* Note that the poisons of envy can be overcome, but with difficulty are laid to rest. *They came together.* That by their multitude they might overcome him whom they could not by reason. In tempting him those come together who in doctrine are contrary to one another. They had already been refuted in the showing of the penny, they had already seen the Sadducees too struck dumb, but yet ill-will and spite nourish shamelessness.

*Tempting him.* Mark says that the Lord said to him, when he had answered wisely: *Thou art not far from the kingdom of God.* For it could come to pass that he who came tempting was converted by the Lord's answer. Or the temptation is not an evil one, as of a man wishing to deceive, but by reason of a man wishing to try out further what he does not know.

*Thou shalt love the Lord thy God.* With his first answer the Lord strikes the feigned conscience of the questioner. *Thy God is one. Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain. Observe the day of the sabbath.* These three belong to the love of God: That thou shouldst think upon his unity, his truth, his will. *With thy whole heart.* The integrity of faith is expressed. In the whole soul, perfect obedience is required. In the whole mind, perseverance is shown.
*Of Christ.* Whether he has come, or whether you believe he is to come, whom you assert to be mere man.
*He said.* To say that is to beget a Son equal to himself. *To my Lord.* Not according to that whereby he was born of him, but according to that whereby he always was of the Father.
*How.* These things are contradictory according to your understanding.
*And no man could,* etc. Note that the poisons of envy can be overcome, but with difficulty are laid to rest.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Which is the great commandment? Love God with all you are.
And love your neighbor as yourself.
Blessed are those who delight in the way of the Lord.
They are like trees planted by streams of water.
On these two commands hang all the law and the prophets.
We will love because God first loved us.
Come, let us worship the God who is love.
We come to love and be made whole. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Picture a tree planted beside a stream, roots drinking deep, leaves green through the dry season, fruit in its time — this is the life rooted in God.
We love because God first loved us.
Love the Lord your God with heart and soul and mind, and love your neighbor as your very self.
We love because God first loved us.
Be holy, for God is holy: deal justly, hold no grudge, lift the fallen, leave room for the poor.
We love because God first loved us.
On these two — love of God, love of neighbor — hangs everything: all the law, all the prophets.
We love because God first loved us.
So come and be planted by the living water, and worship.
We love because God first loved us. Amen.
